note: fine modal shading beyond deduction: will/would for confident inference and characteristic behaviour, should/ought to for expectation rather than advice, can (general possibility) vs may (one occasion), may well / might as well · the raising verbs seem, appear, tend, prove, happen + to-infinitive, incl. the perfect and passive infinitive and negative-on-the-raising-verb · stance adverbs (arguably, presumably, allegedly, reportedly, supposedly, admittedly, understandably, conceivably, undeniably, inevitably, ostensibly, curiously) · hedged commitment frames (likely/unlikely/bound to/certain to, not necessarily, to some extent, in principle, far from, by no means, little doubt, it would appear that) · absorbs the off-path c1_hedging_stance sketch per the registry merge note · deliberately avoids ground owned elsewhere: obligation / permission / advice / deduction / modal perfect (b2_modal_perfect), might-may-must speculation (b1_modals_speculation), impersonal it is said + raised passive reporting (c1_advanced_passive), formal degree adverbs considerably/somewhat/particularly and largely/broadly (c1_register), fronted negative adverbials with inversion (c1_inversion_emphasis), essential/important that + base and were to (c1_subjunctive) · 4 strands x 12 · 48 items · built to live 2026-08-07 (cloud run 16)

cards.title: Modals shade, they do not only rule
cards.body: By C1 the obligation and permission work is done. What is left is the quieter job modals do: shading a plain statement so that a reader hears exactly how sure the writer is. Will and would are the two that catch Czech speakers out, because in these uses neither has anything to do with the future or with conditions. That will be the courier is an inference made now; he will leave his cup on the desk is a habit the speaker finds characteristic; my grandfather would sit there for hours is that same habit in the past. Should and ought to move the other way, from advice towards expectation.
cards.body_cz: Na úrovni C1 je práce s povinností a dovolením hotová. Zbývá tišší úloha modálních sloves: odstínit prostou výpověď tak, aby čtenář slyšel, jak jistý si pisatel je. České mluvčí matou zejména will a would, protože v těchto užitích nemá ani jedno co do činění s budoucností nebo s podmínkou. That will be the courier je úsudek vyslovený nyní; he will leave his cup on the desk je zvyk, který mluvčí pokládá za charakteristický; my grandfather would sit there for hours je týž zvyk v minulosti. Should a ought to se posouvají opačně, od rady k očekávání.

table.caption: the same modal, a different job
rows: That will be my brother at the door.
He will leave his cup on the desk.
My grandfather would sit there for hours.
That would explain the missing file.
The book should arrive on Tuesday.
They ought to be home by now.

points: Ought keeps its to; should never takes one.
Would for a past habit is the written twin of used to, and it needs a repeated action, not a state.
A good teacher will always find a way: will can state a general truth about how the world behaves.

cards.title: can and may split possibility
cards.title_cz: can a may si dělí možnost
cards.body: This is the commonest modal error at C1 and it is invisible to a Czech ear, because both words land on moci. Can describes what happens sometimes, in general, as a property of a thing: winters in Moravia can be very cold says that cold winters occur there. May describes what might happen on one named occasion: it may be cold tomorrow is a forecast about tomorrow. Put can on a specific future occasion and the sentence stops meaning anything a native reader recognises.
cards.body_cz: Toto je nejčastější chyba v modalitě na úrovni C1 a pro české ucho je neviditelná, protože obě slova dopadají na sloveso moci. Can popisuje, co se obecně občas děje, jako vlastnost dané věci: winters in Moravia can be very cold říká, že tam studené zimy nastávají. May popisuje, co se může stát při jedné konkrétní příležitosti: it may be cold tomorrow je předpověď na zítřek. Dosaďte can ke konkrétní budoucí příležitosti a věta přestane znamenat cokoli, co rodilý čtenář rozpozná.

table.caption: general property vs one occasion
rows: Winters here can be very cold.
The meeting may be long today.
The train may be late this evening.

points: May well and could well raise the odds without committing: the delay may well continue for another week.
Might as well is a different phrase again — it means there is no better option available.
Can't in this family denies the possibility outright, which is why it is stronger than may not.

cards.title: seem, appear, tend, prove, happen
cards.body: These five verbs hedge with no modal at all. They borrow a subject that is not theirs — the figures appear to be correct is a claim about the figures, and appear only measures the writer's distance from it. The time sits in the infinitive, not in the verb: he seems to have forgotten reports a past event from the present. The negative belongs to the raising verb, so the company tends not to reply, never the company tends to not reply. Czech reaches for zdá se, že almost every time, and that is why Czech writers over-produce it seems that and under-produce the infinitive pattern.
cards.body_cz: Těchto pět sloves odstiňuje výpověď zcela bez modálního slovesa. Vypůjčují si podmět, který jim nepatří — the figures appear to be correct je tvrzení o číslech a appear jen měří pisatelův odstup od něj. Čas sedí v infinitivu, nikoli ve slovese: he seems to have forgotten referuje z přítomnosti o minulé události. Zápor patří k nadřazenému slovesu, tedy the company tends not to reply, nikdy the company tends to not reply. Čeština sáhne téměř pokaždé po zdá se, že, a proto čeští pisatelé nadužívají it seems that a málo užívají vazbu s infinitivem.

table.caption: one pattern, four shapes
rows: The figures appear to be correct.
He seems to have forgotten the meeting.
The results appear to have been changed.
The company tends not to reply.
There appears to be a mistake.
It seems that no one told the client.

points: Tend to states a tendency, prove to be states how something turned out, happen to marks chance.
There appears to be agrees with the raising verb, not with the noun after it.
Seem also takes a bare adjective: he seemed worried.

cards.title: Stance adverbs: one word of the writer
cards.body: A stance adverb is not a connector. However joins two ideas; arguably grades one. In a single word the writer says how sure they are, whose claim it is, or how they take it. The three groups behave differently and mixing them is what makes a C1 text read as unsure of its own footing: grading down, handing the claim over, and pushing up are three separate moves, and a paragraph should not make all three about the same fact.
cards.body_cz: Postojové příslovce není spojovací výraz. However spojuje dvě myšlenky, arguably jednu odstiňuje. Jediným slovem pisatel sděluje, jak si je jistý, čí je to tvrzení nebo jak je přijímá. Tři skupiny se chovají různě a jejich míchání způsobuje, že text na úrovni C1 působí, jako by si nebyl jistý sám sebou: snížit jistotu, předat tvrzení jinému a jistotu zvýšit jsou tři různé kroky a jeden odstavec by je neměl provést všechny nad týmž faktem.

table.caption: three moves, one word each
rows: hand the claim to someone else

points: Front position with a comma is the default; before the main verb or after be also works.
Allegedly and reportedly are legally load-bearing in journalism — dropping them makes the claim the writer's own.
Ostensibly warns that the stated reason is not the real one; the sentence usually needs a but.

cards.title: Saying how far you will go
cards.body: The last layer is a short list of fixed frames. Likely and unlikely are adjectives, which is why they take is likely to finish and never is probably to finish — the commonest error in the set for Czech writers. Bound to and certain to sit at the strong end. The withdrawing half is the half that is under-used: not necessarily denies the inference rather than the fact, to some extent grants part of the claim, in principle grants it in the abstract, and far from and by no means turn a positive-looking sentence over completely.
cards.body_cz: Poslední vrstvou je krátký seznam pevných rámců. Likely a unlikely jsou přídavná jména, a proto se pojí jako is likely to finish, nikdy is probably to finish — to je pro české pisatele nejčastější chyba v celé skupině. Bound to a certain to stojí na silném konci. Málo užívaná je ustupující polovina: not necessarily popírá úsudek, nikoli fakt, to some extent přiznává část tvrzení, in principle je přiznává v rovině obecné a far from a by no means zdánlivě kladnou větu zcela obrátí.

table.caption: from committed to withdrawn
rows: is bound to · is certain to
denies the inference, not the fact
the most distant frame of all

points: Likely is an adjective in these frames; probably is an adverb and cannot replace it.
In principle concedes the idea and leaves the practice open — it usually earns a but.
By no means and far from are negatives: the sentence around them stays positive in form.

items.en: That will be my brother at the door.
items.cz: To bude můj bratr u dveří.
items.gap: That ____ be my brother at the door.
accepts: That will be my brother at the door.
items.explanation: Beyond the deduction modals a B2 course drills, English uses its modals to shade a statement in ways Czech marks with a particle or with nothing at all. Will and would are the two that surprise Czech speakers most, because neither is about the future or about conditions here: will states a confident inference (that will be my brother at the door) or a characteristic habit (he will leave his cup on the desk), and would does the same job one step back in time or one step less certainly. Should and ought to shift from advice to expectation — the book should arrive on Tuesday is a forecast, not a recommendation. Can and may split the possibility: can is what happens sometimes in general (winters can be cold), may is what might happen on one named occasion (it may be cold tomorrow). Swapping those two is the single commonest modal error at C1.
items.explanation_cz: Vedle dedukčních modálních sloves, která se drilují na úrovni B2, používá angličtina modální slovesa k odstínění výpovědi způsobem, který čeština vyjadřuje částicí nebo vůbec. Nejvíc české mluvčí překvapí will a would, protože zde nejde ani o budoucnost, ani o podmínku: will vyjadřuje jistý úsudek (that will be my brother at the door) nebo charakteristický zvyk (he will leave his cup on the desk) a would dělá totéž o krok zpět v čase nebo o stupeň méně jistě. Should a ought to se posouvají od rady k očekávání — the book should arrive on Tuesday je předpověď, nikoli doporučení. Can a may dělí možnost mezi sebe: can je to, co se obecně občas stává (winters can be cold), may to, co se může stát při jedné konkrétní příležitosti (it may be cold tomorrow). Záměna těchto dvou je nejčastější chybou v modalitě na úrovni C1.

items.explanation: A stance adverb is the writer stepping out from behind the sentence for one word to say how sure they are, or whose claim it is, or how they feel about it. It is not a connector: however joins two ideas, whereas arguably grades one. The set divides cleanly. Arguably, presumably and conceivably grade certainty downwards. Allegedly, reportedly and supposedly hand the claim to someone else, and a journalist who drops them is making the claim themselves. Admittedly and understandably concede. Undeniably and inevitably push upwards. Ostensibly and curiously do something else again: they warn the reader that the writer does not accept what follows at face value. The natural position is the front of the clause with a comma, but a one-word adverb also sits comfortably before the main verb or after be.
items.explanation_cz: Postojové příslovce je pisatel, který na jedno slovo vystoupí zpoza věty, aby řekl, jak si je jistý, čí je to tvrzení nebo jak to na něj působí. Allegedly, reportedly a supposedly předávají tvrzení někomu jinému a novinář, který je vypustí, tvrdí to sám. Admittedly a understandably ustupují a připouštějí. Undeniably a inevitably jistotu naopak zvyšují. Ostensibly a curiously dělají ještě něco jiného: varují čtenáře, že pisatel to, co následuje, nebere za bernou minci.
